keyVerseText: Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron: he: Heb. his soul came into iron
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun כֶּבֶל (kebel) originates from an unused root meaning to twine or braid together, suggesting a binding or fastening by intertwining. This etymology enriches the understanding beyond the simple English term 'fetter' by implying a deliberate, intertwined binding that restricts movement. Such a literal sense of twining or braiding highlights the physical and metaphorical strength of the bonds the word describes.
usageInScripture: The word כֶּבֶל (kebel) appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, consistently translated as 'fetters' or 'bonds.' Both occurrences emphasize physical restraint, often associated with iron chains, underscoring captivity or subjugation. This consistent usage reflects a clear and narrow semantic range focused on tangible bonds, which metaphorically can represent spiritual or moral captivity as well.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding כֶּבֶל as a fetter formed by intertwined bonds deepens the biblical imagery of captivity and deliverance. It reminds believers of the reality of spiritual bondage caused by sin and the power of God to break these fetters, as seen in His redemptive work. The physical imagery of iron fetters conveys the severity of human bondage apart from divine intervention, pointing to Christ as the One who liberates from all chains. This word thus enriches the Christian understanding of bondage and freedom in spiritual terms.
keyVerseReflection: Psalm 105:18 states, 'Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron,' vividly portraying the painful restraint experienced. The use of כֶּבֶל here emphasizes the harshness and reality of physical imprisonment, which metaphorically can reflect the trials and oppression faced by God's people. This word anchors the verse’s message in the tangible experience of suffering, reminding readers of the faithfulness of God even amid severe constraints.
